stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moreno's hypothesis?
stimulus: On rocky reefs off southern California, purple sea urchins can graze kelp forests down to bare rock. Marine ecologist Talia Moreno has observed that kelp tends to be denser on reefs patrolled by the California sheephead, a fish that preys on urchins. Moreno does not credit this pattern to sheephead eating large numbers of urchins. Instead, she hypothesizes that the fish's presence causes urchins to stay hidden in crevices, where they feed on drifting kelp fragments rather than grazing living kelp.
choices: Urchin densities were about the same on reefs with and without sheephead, but urchins on sheephead reefs spent much more of their time sheltered in crevices.
Reefs with sheephead had considerably more living kelp than reefs without sheephead did, and the difference was largest at the shallowest survey sites.
Urchins on both types of reef readily ate drifting kelp fragments whenever such fragments were available to them in crevices or on open rock.
Urchins were the most common prey item found in sheephead stomachs, and urchin densities were much lower on reefs where sheephead were present.
explanation: Moreno's hypothesis has two parts. The kelp difference is not caused by fewer urchins, and it is caused by urchins hiding. Choice A supports both. Urchin numbers match across the two reef types, which rules out predation as the cause, and urchins on sheephead reefs hide far more, which is the behavior Moreno proposes.

B.why: You picked a finding that restates the observation the hypothesis is trying to explain: there is more kelp where sheephead are. It says nothing about why, so it doesn't separate Moreno's explanation from the predation explanation she rejects.

C.why: You picked something that is true of both groups equally. If urchins everywhere eat drifting fragments, this finding can't explain why the two reef types differ. It only shows that urchins can eat fragments, not that sheephead make them hide.

D.why: This finding supports the explanation Moreno explicitly sets aside, that sheephead protect kelp by eating urchins and lowering their numbers. It works against her hypothesis.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the research team's conclusion?
stimulus: In a twelve-week trial, adults who took a daily inulin supplement showed smaller rises in blood glucose after meals than adults who took a placebo. Human enzymes cannot digest inulin. Instead, gut bacteria ferment it and release compounds such as butyrate. The research team concluded that inulin blunted the glucose rises not directly but through the butyrate that bacteria produced from it.
choices: Inulin participants' glucose rises after meals shrank steadily across the twelve weeks, while placebo participants' rises stayed about the same throughout.
Inulin participants given an antibiotic that suppressed gut bacteria produced little butyrate and had glucose rises similar to placebo participants' rises.
Blood butyrate levels increased by similar amounts in the inulin participants and the placebo participants over the course of the twelve-week trial.
Inulin participants reported feeling fuller after meals and, on average, ate smaller portions than placebo participants did at nearly every meal.
explanation: The conclusion is a chain: inulin leads to bacterial butyrate, and butyrate leads to smaller glucose rises. Inulin alone is not supposed to do it. Choice B removes the middle link while keeping the inulin. With bacteria suppressed, butyrate stays low and the benefit disappears. That shows the effect depends on butyrate, just as the team concluded.

A.why: You picked a finding that restates the observed result, that inulin users had smaller glucose rises. It never mentions butyrate, so it can't show that butyrate is the cause.

C.why: If butyrate rose equally in both groups, butyrate can't explain why only the inulin group improved. This finding is true of both groups equally and undercuts the proposed mechanism.

D.why: This points to a different cause, eating less, rather than the butyrate mechanism the team proposed. A competing explanation doesn't support their conclusion.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Arata's conclusion?
stimulus: Soft, water-saturated ground can intensify earthquake shaking, but it does not do so evenly. After a moderate earthquake struck near a coastal city, seismologist Kenji Arata compared recordings from instruments on artificially reclaimed harbor land with recordings from instruments on nearby bedrock. Arata concluded that the reclaimed land amplified slow, long-period ground motion but had little effect on rapid, short-period motion.
choices: Overall peak shaking at the reclaimed-land stations was greater than at the bedrock stations, and several harbor structures were damaged during the earthquake.
Reclaimed-land stations recorded about three times the bedrock stations' motion at both long periods and short periods throughout the earthquake.
Reclaimed-land stations recorded about three times the bedrock stations' long-period motion but roughly the same short-period motion as the bedrock stations.
Reclaimed-land stations recorded about the same long-period motion as the bedrock stations but roughly three times their short-period motion.
explanation: Arata's conclusion has two parts: amplification at long periods and little or no amplification at short periods. Choice C confirms both. It is the only choice that separates the two kinds of motion the way the conclusion does.

A.why: You picked a finding that confirms only that the reclaimed land shook more overall. It doesn't distinguish long-period motion from short-period motion, which is the whole point of the conclusion.

B.why: This supports a broader claim, that the reclaimed land amplifies all shaking. Arata said short-period motion was barely affected, so amplification at both periods goes against the limit set by the word 'but'.

D.why: This reverses the two parts. It puts the amplification at short periods and none at long periods, the opposite of what Arata concluded.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's conclusion?
stimulus: When wildfire burns intensely, waxy compounds vaporized from plant litter can condense on cooler soil grains below the surface and form a layer that repels water. Rain that would normally soak in then runs off the slope. After a fire swept unevenly through the Alder Creek basin, hydrologist Rosa Lindqvist concluded that the basin's sharply increased storm runoff came mainly from its severely burned slopes, not from its lightly burned ones.
choices: Storm runoff from the Alder Creek basin after the fire was roughly double the runoff produced by similar storms in the years before the fire.
Soil samples from severely and lightly burned slopes showed water-repellent layers of similar strength and absorbed similar amounts of simulated rain.
Severely burned slopes in several other basins that burned the same year also developed water-repellent layers within a few weeks of the fire.
Soil from severely burned slopes had a strong water-repellent layer and absorbed little simulated rain, while soil from lightly burned slopes absorbed rain normally.
explanation: Lindqvist's conclusion contrasts two groups of slopes: severely burned slopes produced the runoff and lightly burned slopes did not. Choice D separates them in exactly that way. It also links each group to the middle step of the passage's chain, the water-repellent layer that turns rain into runoff.

A.why: You picked a finding that restates the observed result, that runoff increased. It treats the basin as a whole, so it can't show which slopes the extra water came from.

B.why: This finding is true of both groups equally. If both kinds of slope repel water to the same degree, nothing explains why the severely burned slopes would produce most of the runoff. It undercuts the contrast in the conclusion.

C.why: You went beyond the basin Lindqvist studied. Findings from other basins say nothing about how severely and lightly burned slopes in Alder Creek compare.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nandakumar's claim?
stimulus: Concrete inevitably cracks, and water seeping into the cracks corrodes the steel reinforcement inside. Materials engineer Priya Nandakumar prepared two sets of concrete beams that were identical except that one set contained dormant bacterial spores and a calcium-based nutrient. When water enters a crack, the spores revive and deposit calcium carbonate. After cracking both sets and keeping them wet for six weeks, Nandakumar claimed that the bacteria enabled the concrete to seal narrow cracks but provided no benefit for wide ones.
choices: Narrow cracks in the bacterial beams sealed completely within the six weeks, and calcium carbonate deposits were found lining the sealed cracks.
Narrow cracks sealed in the bacterial beams but not in the ordinary beams, while wide cracks stayed open in both sets of beams.
Both narrow and wide cracks sealed in the bacterial beams, while neither narrow nor wide cracks sealed in the ordinary beams.
Narrow cracks sealed in both the bacterial beams and the ordinary beams, while wide cracks stayed open in both sets of beams.
explanation: The claim has two parts. For narrow cracks, the bacterial beams do better than the ordinary ones. For wide cracks, the two sets show no difference. Choice B confirms both parts and compares the matched groups, so the sealing can be credited to the bacteria, the only thing that differed.

A.why: You picked a finding that confirms only one part. It shows that narrow cracks sealed in the bacterial beams, but without the ordinary beams you can't tell whether the bacteria made a difference, and it says nothing about wide cracks.

C.why: This supports a stronger claim than Nandakumar made, that the bacteria help with all cracks. She said they provide no benefit for wide cracks, so this finding goes beyond her claim.

D.why: This finding is true of both groups equally. If ordinary beams sealed narrow cracks just as well, the bacteria made no difference, which contradicts the first part of the claim.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?
stimulus: Sports scientists assigned recreational runners to one of two six-week programs with the same weekly distance and pace. One group ran on uneven forest trails; the other ran on a flat track. During the following season, the trail runners suffered fewer ankle sprains. The researchers concluded that trail running prevented sprains by strengthening the small muscles that stabilize the ankle, not simply by making runners fitter overall.
choices: Trail runners reported fewer ankle sprains than track runners did, both during the program and in the season that followed it.
Trail runners gained more ankle-stabilizer strength than track runners did, while the two groups' aerobic fitness improved by similar amounts.
Trail runners improved their aerobic fitness more than track runners did, while the two groups gained similar ankle-stabilizer strength.
Runners in both groups who had sprained an ankle before the program were more likely than others to sprain one again later.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts: trail running strengthened the ankle stabilizers, and the benefit did not come from general fitness. Choice B confirms both. Trail runners gained more stabilizer strength, and fitness improved equally in both groups, so fitness can't explain the difference.

A.why: You picked a choice that restates the observed result, fewer sprains. The researchers already knew that. Their conclusion is about why it happened, and this choice says nothing about ankle muscles or fitness.

C.why: You matched the right variables but missed the direction. If fitness rose more for trail runners and stabilizer strength was the same in both groups, then fitness explains the result better than muscle strength does. That is the opposite of what the researchers concluded.

D.why: You chose a finding that is true of both groups equally. Because it doesn't separate trail runners from track runners, it can't show what trail running did.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?
stimulus: Hydrologists monitored two small streams in neighboring valleys with similar soils, slopes and rainfall. One stream had a series of beaver dams; the other had none. By late August, the undammed stream had shrunk to isolated pools, while the dammed stream was still flowing. The team concluded that the ponds behind the dams raise the surrounding water table, and that this stored groundwater then seeps back into the stream during dry months.
choices: In late August, the dammed stream carried measurable flow along its full length, while the undammed stream did not.
Between June and August, water tables in both valleys fell by similar amounts, as they do in most years in the region.
Water spilling over the tops of the dams supplied most of the dammed stream's August flow, with little coming from the ground.
Wells beside the dammed stream had higher water tables than wells in the other valley, and groundwater supplied most of its August flow.
explanation: The conclusion is a chain: dams raise the water table, and that groundwater feeds the stream in dry months. Choice D supports both links. The water table is higher near the dammed stream, and groundwater makes up most of that stream's late-summer flow.

A.why: You picked a choice that restates the observed result, that the dammed stream kept flowing. The conclusion explains why it kept flowing, and this choice never mentions the water table or groundwater.

B.why: You chose a pattern shared equally by both valleys. A change that happens the same way with or without dams can't show what the dams do.

C.why: You accepted a different mechanism. In this choice, surface water spilling over the dams feeds the stream and groundwater contributes little. That goes against the team's groundwater explanation.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Oyelaran's hypothesis?
stimulus: Chemically strengthened glass is made by soaking glass in a molten salt bath, which swaps small sodium ions near the surface for larger potassium ions. The crowded surface layer is squeezed into compression. Materials scientist Tomasz Oyelaran hypothesizes that this layer helps glass resist sharp, shallow contacts, such as scratches from sand, but offers little benefit against blunt impacts, which stress the glass well below its thin treated surface.
choices: Treated panes cracked far less often than untreated panes when dragged across sand, but the two broke at similar rates when struck by a steel ball.
Treated panes cracked far less often than untreated panes both when dragged across sand and when struck by a steel ball.
Treated and untreated panes alike cracked more often when struck by a steel ball than when they were dragged across sand.
Treated panes held more potassium near their surfaces than untreated panes did, though their interiors were nearly identical.
explanation: The hypothesis makes a contrast with two parts: the treatment helps against scratches, and it helps little against blunt impacts. Choice A confirms both. Treated glass does better on sand and no better against the steel ball.

B.why: You confirmed only the first part of the hypothesis. A benefit against steel-ball impacts goes against the claim that the treatment offers little help with blunt impacts.

C.why: You chose a pattern that is true of treated and untreated glass alike. It compares the two kinds of contact but not the two kinds of glass, so it says nothing about what the treatment does.

D.why: You picked a restatement of how the treatment works, which the passage already describes. The hypothesis is about how treated glass performs, and this choice gives no performance results.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's prediction?
stimulus: When soil is wet, part of the sun's energy goes into evaporating water rather than heating the ground, which keeps the air above it cooler. Climatologist Renata Okafor found that summer afternoons in an irrigated farming district were cooler than in a nearby rain-fed district. She predicts that if the district's farmers replace sprinklers with drip lines, which wet much less of the soil surface, its afternoons will grow warmer.
choices: Over the summer, afternoon temperatures in the irrigated district averaged several degrees below those in the rain-fed district.
Afternoon temperatures in both districts climbed by similar amounts during weeks when little or no rain fell.
Within the irrigated district, drip-watered fields had warmer afternoons than sprinkler-watered fields, nearer to rain-fed levels.
Within the irrigated district, drip-watered fields had cooler afternoons than sprinkler-watered fields despite drier soil surfaces.
explanation: The prediction connects one cause to one outcome: drip lines leave less wet soil, so afternoons get warmer. Choice C tests exactly that switch. Fields that already use drip lines are warmer than sprinkler-watered fields, which is what the prediction expects.

A.why: You picked the earlier observation that the prediction starts from. Knowing that the irrigated district is cooler doesn't show that changing the watering method would warm it.

B.why: You chose a pattern shared equally by both districts. A change that affects both the same way doesn't separate sprinklers from drip lines.

D.why: You got the direction backward. If drip-watered fields are cooler, then switching to drip lines would cool the afternoons, not warm them as Okafor predicts.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's hypothesis?
stimulus: Corals on shallow reef flats endure daily temperature swings of several degrees, while corals of the same species a few meters deeper live in steadier water. During marine heatwaves, the reef-flat corals bleach less often. Marine biologist Kai Lindqvist hypothesizes that this tolerance is not inherited but acquired: corals become more heat tolerant through repeated exposure to fluctuating temperatures.
choices: During the most recent marine heatwave, a smaller share of reef-flat corals than of deeper corals bleached.
Deep-water fragments moved to the reef flat for a year later bleached less in heated tanks than deep fragments left in place.
Reef-flat and deep-water colonies of the species were found to differ in several genes linked to heat tolerance.
Reef-flat and deep-water corals regained their color at similar rates in the months after the heatwave ended.
explanation: The hypothesis says tolerance comes from exposure, not inheritance. Choice B moves deep-water corals with the same origin into fluctuating water. Only the moved fragments gained tolerance, so the difference comes from exposure and not from the corals' origin.

A.why: You picked a choice that restates the observed result, that reef-flat corals bleach less. The hypothesis tries to explain why, and this choice doesn't separate inheritance from exposure.

C.why: You picked evidence for the explanation the hypothesis rejects. Genetic differences linked to heat tolerance point toward inherited tolerance, not acquired tolerance.

D.why: You chose a feature the two groups share equally. Similar recovery rates don't distinguish the groups, and recovery after bleaching isn't the tolerance the hypothesis is about.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's conclusion?
stimulus: Damselfish farm small patches of algae on coral reefs and chase away other fish that try to graze there. At two reefs off the coast of Belize, marine biologist Inés Calderón saw that damselfish at Reef A chased intruders far more aggressively than damselfish at Reef B did, even though the two reefs had similar numbers of grazing fish. Most of Reef A's branching coral had been destroyed in a storm. Calderón concluded that the Reef A damselfish defend more fiercely because good algae patches are scarcer there, not because intruders arrive more often.
choices: At Reef A, damselfish chased intruders more often and over longer distances than damselfish at Reef B did over the same observation periods.
At Reef A, damselfish holding small algae patches defended them harder than those holding large patches, though intruders visited both equally often.
At Reef A, intruding fish entered damselfish territories much more often than at Reef B, especially near the coral damaged by the storm.
At both reefs, damselfish chased intruders that eat algae more often than they chased intruders that feed mainly on drifting plankton.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts: aggression rises because algae patches are scarce, and it does not rise because intruders come more often. Choice B ties how hard a fish defends to how much algae it holds, and it keeps the number of intruders the same. That supports the proposed cause and rules out the rival one at once.

A.why: This only repeats the observation the passage opens with: Reef A fish are more aggressive. It says nothing about why, so it can't support one explanation over the other.

C.why: This points to the explanation Calderón rejects, more frequent intruders. It also clashes with the passage's statement that the two reefs had similar numbers of grazing fish. It would weaken the conclusion, not support it.

D.why: This is true of both reefs in the same way, so it can't explain why Reef A fish behave differently from Reef B fish. A finding that fits both groups equally doesn't separate them.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the ornithologist's hypothesis?
stimulus: On Arctic tundra, an early snowmelt brings the summer peak in insects forward, and shorebird chicks that hatch after that peak find less food and grow more slowly. Semipalmated sandpipers decide when to nest by day length, which is the same every year. Dunlins decide by local air temperature. Ornithologist Pavel Lindqvist hypothesizes that in early-melt years, sandpiper chicks will leave the nest lighter than usual, while dunlin chicks will not.
choices: In early-melt years, both sandpiper and dunlin chicks left the nest noticeably lighter than chicks of their species raised in late-melt years.
In early-melt years, sandpiper chicks hatched later relative to the insect peak than they did in years when the snow melted late.
In early-melt years, sandpiper chicks hatched after the insect peak and left the nest lighter, while dunlin chicks hatched earlier and kept typical weights.
Across the study years, dunlins began nesting earlier in warm springs than in cold ones, while sandpipers began nesting on about the same date.
explanation: The hypothesis predicts a contrast. In early-melt years, sandpiper chicks should be lighter, and dunlin chicks should not be. Choice C confirms both halves. It also shows the middle step the passage describes: sandpipers miss the insect peak and dunlins, nesting earlier, don't.

A.why: If dunlin chicks are also lighter, the predicted difference between the two species disappears. This finding goes against the hypothesis's claim that dunlins will not be affected.

B.why: This supports only the middle link for one species. It says nothing about chick weight and nothing about dunlins, so it confirms just one part of a two-part prediction.

D.why: This restates the background the passage already gives about how each species times its nesting. It doesn't show the predicted outcome, the difference in chick weight.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hydrologist's claim?
stimulus: During a long drought in the Rocky Mountain foothills, stretches of stream below beaver dams kept flowing for weeks after nearby undammed stretches had gone dry. One explanation is simply that the ponds behind the dams held water and slowly spilled it downstream. Hydrologist Mara Okafor disagrees. She claims that the ponds kept the streams alive mainly by pushing water into the shallow ground nearby, which then seeped back into the channel as the drought went on.
choices: During the drought, the stretches below beaver dams kept flowing for several weeks after the nearby undammed stretches had stopped flowing entirely.
At the start of the drought, the beaver ponds held millions of liters of water, and most of it spilled over the dams into the stream by midsummer.
Late in the drought, wells near the dams held more water than wells near undammed stretches, and most streamflow entered through the streambed.
Streams in other mountain watersheds that contain beaver dams have also kept flowing through droughts that dried up nearby undammed streams.
explanation: Okafor's claim is a chain. The ponds push water into the ground, and that groundwater later seeps back into the stream. Choice C shows both links. There was more groundwater near the dams, and the late-season flow came up through the streambed rather than over the dams, which separates her explanation from the spillover one.

A.why: This only repeats the observation both explanations are trying to account for. Because it fits either one equally well, it gives no support to Okafor's in particular.

B.why: Water spilling over the dams is the rival explanation that Okafor rejects. This finding supports the view she argues against.

D.why: This extends the observation to other watersheds, but it still doesn't show how the water got into the streams. A wider pattern doesn't establish the groundwater mechanism.

stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT support the team's conclusion?
stimulus: Plants take in carbon dioxide through tiny pores called stomata, and many species grow fewer stomata when CO2 is plentiful, since fewer openings are then needed. Paleobotanist Lindiwe Sithole and colleagues counted stomata on fossil ginkgo leaves from two rock layers in a single outcrop. Leaves from the younger layer had far fewer stomata than leaves from the older layer. Dry conditions can also reduce stomatal counts, so the team considered drought as a cause. They concluded, however, that the decline reflects a rise in atmospheric CO2.
choices: Pollen in the younger layer comes mostly from ferns and mosses that grow only in places with steady, year-round moisture.
Soil minerals in the younger layer have carbon isotope ratios indicating more atmospheric CO2 than those in the older layer.
Ginkgo leaves in the younger layer have fewer stomata per square millimeter of leaf surface than ginkgo leaves in the older layer.
A fern whose stomata respond to CO2 but not to moisture also has fewer stomata in the younger layer than in the older one.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts. The decline was caused by rising CO2, and it was not caused by drought. Choice C only says again what the team already observed: the younger leaves have fewer stomata. It doesn't tell you anything about why. Both CO2 and drought could produce that result, so it does nothing to separate the two explanations and gives no support to the team's conclusion.

A.why: You may have dismissed this as a side detail about pollen. But plants that need constant moisture show that the younger layer formed in wet conditions. That rules out drought, which is one of the two things the conclusion needs, so this finding does support it.

B.why: You may have thought soil chemistry was too indirect to say anything about the leaves. But the conclusion is about higher CO2 in the younger layer's time. Independent evidence that CO2 really was higher then supports the proposed cause directly.

D.why: You may have read this as being about a different plant and so beside the point. But a species that reacts only to CO2 shows the same drop in the same layer. That points to CO2 and not drought, which is exactly the separation the conclusion needs.

stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT support Brezina's conclusion?
stimulus: Traffic noise is loudest at low frequencies, so it can drown out the lower notes of birdsong. Ornithologist Hana Brezina recorded song sparrows in twelve city parks: six beside highways and six of matching size and vegetation far from any road. Males in the highway parks sang songs whose lowest notes were noticeably higher in pitch. Brezina concluded that the noise itself pushes the birds' songs upward, rather than the two groups simply having inherited different local song traditions.
choices: Males in quiet parks raised the lowest notes of their songs when researchers played recordings of highway traffic nearby.
Males in highway parks and in quiet parks sang at similar rates and for similar lengths of time each morning.
Males in highway parks lowered the lowest notes of their songs on holidays, when traffic on the highways was light.
Males in one highway park lowered the lowest notes of their songs after a new sound wall cut the noise there.
explanation: Brezina's conclusion needs evidence that noise causes the pitch shift and that inherited song tradition doesn't. Choice B describes something that is the same in both groups: how often and how long the birds sing. A feature both groups share can't explain how they differ, and it says nothing about either noise or tradition. So it gives no support.

A.why: You may have thought quiet-park birds were the wrong group to look at. But when noise is added and those same birds raise their pitch, you can see noise causing the shift directly. An inherited tradition couldn't change that quickly, so this supports the conclusion.

C.why: You may have noticed that the birds lowered their pitch and taken that as working against the conclusion. In fact, the pitch fell exactly when the noise fell. That tracks noise, not a fixed tradition, so it supports Brezina's explanation.

D.why: You may have decided that one park was too small a sample to count. But the question asks only whether a finding supports the conclusion, not whether it proves it. When the same birds change their songs as soon as the noise is removed, that supports noise as the cause.

stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT support the researchers' prediction?
stimulus: In mountain basins, the date when winter snowpack melts shapes conditions months later. When snow melts early, plants leaf out sooner and draw water from the soil over a longer season. Climatologist Arturo Quispe and colleagues studied two neighboring basins of similar elevation and vegetation. Snow melted in early April in the Rito basin but in late May in the Calera basin. The team predicted that by late August, Rito's soils would be drier than Calera's, mainly because of the longer period of plant water use.
choices: Plants in the Rito basin began drawing water from the soil weeks earlier than plants in Calera, though summer rain was similar.
In past years when the Calera basin's snow melted in April, its late-August soils were about as dry as Rito's usually are.
Test plots in the Rito basin that were cleared of plants after snowmelt stayed as moist through August as soils in Calera.
Soils in both basins were soaked with meltwater for several weeks immediately after the snow there had disappeared.
explanation: The prediction links a chain of causes: early melt leads to a longer period of plant water use, which leads to drier soils in late August. It also says Rito will differ from Calera. Choice D describes something both basins share, wet soils right after the melt. It doesn't separate the basins or show the plant link in the chain, so it gives no support.

A.why: You may have read this as only a timing detail. But it shows the middle link in the chain, longer plant water use in Rito. It also rules out rainfall as an alternative explanation, so it supports the prediction.

B.why: You may have thought data from earlier years couldn't speak to this year. But when Calera's snow melted early in the past, its soils dried out like Rito's. That ties early melt to late-summer dryness, which supports the prediction.

C.why: You may have read 'stayed moist' as working against a prediction about drier soils. But removing the plants stopped the drying. That isolates plant water use as the cause, which is exactly the mechanism the team proposed.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the health officials' conclusion?
stimulus: In the fall of 2023, a county health department texted flu-shot reminders to residents of two similar towns. The message sent to Alder named a nearby pharmacy and listed its hours; the message sent to Brisk said only that shots were available locally. Vaccination rose in both towns, but it rose more in Alder. Health officials concluded that the added detail helped mainly by sparing residents the effort of finding out where to go.
choices: In both Alder and Brisk, vaccination rose by more than it did in a nearby town of similar size whose residents received no reminder message at all.
Among residents who had not known where to get a shot, the increase was much larger in Alder than in Brisk, but among those who already knew, it was similar.
Among residents who already knew where to get a shot, the increase was much larger in Alder than in Brisk, but among those who had not known, it was similar.
A larger share of Alder residents than of Brisk residents received a flu shot during the month after the reminder messages were sent out by text.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts: the pharmacy detail made the difference, and it worked by saving people the effort of finding a place to go. If that is the mechanism, the gap between the towns should show up among people who didn't know where to go, and should mostly disappear among people who already knew. Choice B reports exactly that pattern, so it ties the cause to the outcome.

A.why: This is true of both towns equally. It shows that reminders help in general, but it says nothing about why Alder's increase was larger than Brisk's, so it doesn't support the explanation for the gap.

C.why: You got the direction backward. If the gap appeared only among people who already knew where to go, the detail could not have worked by saving them the search. That would weaken the officials' explanation.

D.why: This just restates the result the passage already gives, which is that Alder's rate rose more. It doesn't show the mechanism the officials propose, so it adds no support.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's claim?
stimulus: In the 1830s, handloom weavers in two neighboring towns obtained yarn in different ways. In Brennick, most bought it on credit from a single merchant who also purchased their finished cloth; in Tessel, most paid cash for yarn at an open market. Over the decade, Brennick's cloth became far more uniform in width and color than Tessel's. Historian Ada Lindqvist argues that the credit arrangement produced this difference by letting the merchant dictate standards that weavers had to meet.
choices: Cloth from both Brennick and Tessel sold at noticeably higher prices at the end of the decade than it had at the start of the decade.
Tessel's market officials enforced standard widths for all cloth sold there, while the Brennick merchant accepted cloth of any width.
The Brennick merchant's ledgers record refusing pieces that missed set widths, while Tessel's market records show no pieces turned away.
By the end of the decade, Brennick's cloth was much closer to a single standard width than Tessel's cloth was, judging by surviving samples.
explanation: Lindqvist's claim is a chain: credit gave the merchant control, the merchant used that control to set standards, and the standards made the cloth uniform. Choice C supplies the middle link for Brennick, where the merchant rejected pieces that missed the standard, and shows that Tessel had no such pressure. That explains why the two towns differed.

A.why: This finding applies to both towns equally, so it can't explain why one town's cloth became uniform and the other's did not.

B.why: This reverses the claim. It puts the enforced standards in Tessel and takes them away from the Brennick merchant, which would undercut the idea that the merchant's control produced the uniformity.

D.why: This only restates the observed result, that Brennick's cloth was more uniform. It doesn't show that the credit arrangement or the merchant's standards caused it.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's claim?
stimulus: In 1892 a publisher issued an inexpensive songbook containing forty of the ballads then sung in a rural region, with each melody printed in notation. When folklorists recorded singers there in the 1920s, they found far fewer melodic variants of the songbook ballads than of ballads the book had omitted. Musicologist Tomás Ferreira argues that the printed notation itself slowed the melodies' drift, and that the gap does not simply reflect which ballads were most popular.
choices: Before 1892, the ballads chosen for the songbook were already sung far more widely in the region than the ballads that it omitted.
Recordings from the 1920s include far fewer melodic variants of the songbook ballads than of the ballads that the songbook omitted.
Ballads in both groups had more melodic variants in the 1920s recordings than in transcriptions made in the region in the 1880s.
Among ballads equally widely sung before 1892, those in the songbook had far fewer variants by the 1920s than those it omitted.
explanation: Ferreira's claim has two parts: printing slowed the drift, and popularity does not explain the gap. To support both, a finding has to hold popularity constant and still show the difference. Choice D compares ballads that were equally popular, and the printed ones still had fewer variants. That points to the notation as the cause.

A.why: This supports the explanation Ferreira rejects. If the songbook ballads were already the most popular, popularity could account for the gap, which weakens the claim that the notation itself mattered.

B.why: This repeats the result the passage already reports. It doesn't separate printing from popularity, so it gives no support to Ferreira's explanation.

C.why: This is true of both groups, so it describes something they share, not the gap between them. It can't show that printing made the difference.
